notes.meaning: God points to His chosen Servant. Matthew 12:17-21 says this was fulfilled in Jesus. Jesus willingly took the role of a servant. The Father holds Him up, delights in Him, and gives Him the Holy Spirit, echoed by the voice from heaven at His baptism. He brings God's justice, God's right way of living, to the nations (the Gentiles, or non-Jewish peoples), not just to Israel.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament adds the names "Jacob" and "Israel" here. That makes the Servant the nation of Israel.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many scholars think a second, later prophet wrote these chapters of Isaiah. They count verses 1-7 as the first of four "servant songs."

notes.meaning: The Servant comes quietly, without the noise and show of earthly kings. He does not shout to make Himself famous. Jesus often told people not to spread the news of His miracles. It does not mean He never raised His voice. It describes His humble, gentle way.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The older Catholic Douay-Rheims Bible words part of this verse as "nor have respect to person."

notes.meaning: A bruised reed is a weak, hurting person. A smoldering wick is faith that is almost out. Jesus does not crush such people. He strengthens them and gently fans the little flame back to life. Yet He brings justice in truth, so His kindness never excuses sin. Some older writers add that He is also patient with the wicked, giving them time to turn back.

In Hebrew, the words for "grow weak" and "discouraged" echo the dim wick and the bruised reed. The Servant pities weakness but is never weak Himself. He keeps going until God's justice is set up on the earth. He does this through His life, His cross and the spread of the gospel. The "islands," meaning faraway lands, long for His teaching and will welcome it.

Before making His promise, God shows who He is. He made the heavens and the earth, and He gives breath to every person. The One who did all that surely has the power to keep His word and support His Servant. Saving people brings them back to the God who made them.

God now speaks to the Servant directly. He has called Him for a right purpose and will hold His hand and guard Him. A covenant is a binding promise-relationship between God and His people. God makes the Servant that covenant in person, as well as its go-between. He is also a light for the nations living in spiritual darkness.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: The Hebrew word behind "keep" is uncertain. Some Bibles read it as "protect" and others as "form."

notes.meaning: The Servant opens blind eyes and sets prisoners free. Jesus did heal blind people, but the deeper meaning is spiritual. He opens minds that Satan has blinded and frees people from the prison of sin. Cyrus could only open the prison doors for the exiles. Christ, by His grace, actually brings people out.

"The LORD" stands for God's own personal name. It marks Him as the one true God, who never changes. He will not share His glory with idols. His glory is seen in keeping His promises, so He will surely do what He said. The Son shares the Father's glory (John 17:5), which shows that both are the LORD.

The "former things" are God's earlier predictions, which have already come true. The "new things" are fresh promises: the Messiah, God's promised Savior, and the nations turning to God. God tells about them before they sprout, like a plant before it shows a bud. Only the true God can do that, so we can trust Him for the future.

A new kind of mercy calls for a new song. Before, God's praise was sung mostly in Israel. Now it will rise from the ends of the earth. Sailors, the creatures of the sea, and faraway islands are all called to join in. The reason is the salvation of the world through Christ.

The call to praise moves east into the desert. Kedar was a group of Arab tribes living in tents and villages. Sela was the rock city of Edom, known as Petra. With the islands to the west, praise will be heard from sunrise to sunset. Even remote and rough peoples will give God glory when the good news reaches them.

God goes out like a mighty warrior with a battle cry. His zeal is His burning love for His people and His honor. First, He would defeat Babylon to free Israel. Christian writers also see a picture of the gospel defeating Satan's kingdom. Either way, His people can count on His strength.

God says He has held back for a long time. The years of exile felt like forever to His loving heart. Now He cries out like a woman giving birth. Something great He has long been carrying is about to be born. The picture shows the depth of His love and how urgently He will act.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: The ancient translations read the last words as "destroy and devour." Most modern scholars read "pant and gasp," as this Bible does.

notes.meaning: Turning mountains to waste and rivers to dry land is picture language. God will bring down the proud powers holding His people captive and clear every obstacle from their path home. No army or defense can stop Him when He sets out to rescue His people.

God leads the "blind" by roads they never knew. First, He led the exiles home. He also leads helpless people who cannot see a way out, showing them the way of life through Jesus. He turns their darkness to light and smooths the rough places. He promises never to leave them.

People who call metal statues their gods will be turned back in shame. Their idols cannot help them. Only those who trust the true God will be saved. Anything we trust in place of God becomes an idol.

God now calls to those who are deaf and blind by choice. This blindness is not the helpless kind of verse 16. These people simply refuse to see. It is like Jesus telling the man with a withered hand to stretch it out. God calls us to do what we cannot do alone, and then gives the power to do it.

Here "My servant" means the nation of Israel, along with its priests and teachers. They were meant to carry God's truth to the world, but they had become blind and deaf to Him. Those who have the most light are the least excused when they close their eyes. The word for "covenant partner" is hard to translate. It may mean "perfect one" or "friend."

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The older Catholic Douay-Rheims Bible reads "he that is sold" in place of "he that is perfect."

notes.meaning: Israel saw many proofs of God's goodness and heard the prophets, but did not take it to heart. People are often lost not because they never knew, but because they did not care. Jesus described the people of His day the same way (Matthew 13:14-15).

God gave Israel a great and glorious law, His teaching through Moses and the prophets. He did it for the sake of His own righteousness and faithfulness, not because Israel deserved it. Christians see this fulfilled in Christ, who kept the law perfectly. In Him, God saves sinners and still honors His justice.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: One Catholic translation, the Catholic Public Domain Version, reads "the Lord was willing to sanctify him."

notes.meaning: Even after all God gave them, Israel was robbed and trapped, with no one to rescue them. This came because of their sin and unbelief. It happened first in the exile to Babylon. Some older writers also see the later fall of Jerusalem to the Romans. It pictures spiritual captivity too.

The question is really a longing wish: "Oh, that someone would listen!" God wants His people to learn from what has happened and obey from now on. His discipline is not revenge. It is meant to warn and guide us for the future.

Israel's disaster was not bad luck. The LORD allowed it because they sinned and would not walk in His ways. The prophet says "we," counting himself among the sinners. God's anger came like war and fire, yet the people were like someone in a burning house who does not notice. When hard times come, we should look to God and turn back to Him.
